title: Skilled Trades
tagline: Electrician, plumber, HVAC, welding, automotive — earn while you learn in careers that can't be offshored.
summary: Skilled trades are licensed, hands-on careers learned primarily through paid apprenticeships rather than four-year degrees — with strong demand and clear ladders from helper to journeyman to master to business owner. This roadmap covers the apprenticeship model, the major trades, licensing, and the business side.

detail.description: Skilled trades are careers built on licenses and hands-on mastery — electrical, plumbing, HVAC, welding, automotive and more. You earn while you learn through apprenticeships instead of paying for a four-year degree.
detail.why: Demand is strong and supply of new tradespeople is short; for people who like tangible work, trades offer early income, durable skills, and a real ownership path.
learn: Read the BLS OOH profiles for electricians and plumbers
Browse apprenticeship.gov for registered programs near you
Talk to one tradesperson about a typical week and body impact
List your constraints: physical work, hours, on-call, weather

detail.description: Registered apprenticeships combine paid on-the-job training (typically 2–5 years) with related classroom instruction, run by unions, employers, or trade schools, and end with journeyman-level credentials.
detail.why: Apprenticeship is the on-ramp for nearly every trade — understanding how to get selected (aptitude tests, interviews, physical readiness) is step one.
learn: Compare union vs open-shop (non-union) apprenticeships
Learn the typical structure: OJT hours + classroom hours per year
Prepare for common entry tests (basic math, mechanical aptitude)
Apply to 3+ programs; treat it like a job search

detail.description: Safety is the first trade skill: OSHA 10/30-hour construction or general-industry cards, PPE discipline, lockout/tagout awareness, ladder and trenching basics.
detail.why: OSHA cards are hiring prerequisites on most sites, and safe habits are what keep a 30-year career possible.
learn: Complete an OSHA 10-hour course (or OSHA 30 for supervisors)
Learn PPE selection for your trade's common hazards
Understand lockout/tagout basics for energized equipment
Practice spotting hazards on any site you visit

certs.name: OSHA 10 / OSHA 30
certs.note: 10-hour (entry) and 30-hour (supervisor) safety courses; widely required on US job sites.

detail.description: Each trade has different work environments, physical demands, licensure depth, and pay ceilings: electrical and plumbing carry the deepest licensing; HVAC and automotive emphasize equipment; welding spans fabrication industries.
detail.why: Your trade choice is a decade-shaping decision — match it to your body, interests, and local market rather than general pay rankings.
learn: Shadow or job-site-tour two trades if possible
Compare apprenticeship lengths and licensing steps per trade
Check your local demand: which trades are short-handed?
Rank trades on indoor/outdoor, on-call, and complexity fit

detail.description: Electricians install and maintain power, lighting, and control systems — apprenticeship (commonly ~4 years / 8,000 OJT hours), journeyman exam, optional master license, and specialties from residential to industrial controls.
detail.why: Electrical is one of the deepest-licensed trades with strong demand from electrification, solar, and data-center construction.
learn: Learn the apprentice → journeyman → master ladder in your state
Study basic electrical theory (Ohm's law, circuits) before applying
Compare residential, commercial, and industrial niches
Note state licensing board requirements and exam outlines
tasks: Install, maintain, and repair electrical wiring, equipment, and fixtures, ensuring that work is in accordance with relevant codes.

detail.description: Plumbers and pipefitters install water, drainage, and gas systems — apprenticeship (~4–5 years), journeyman license, optional master, with niches in service, new construction, medical gas, and steamfitting.
detail.why: Plumbing is recession-resistant (everything leaks eventually) and among the strongest trades for eventual business ownership.
learn: Map your state's plumber licensing tiers
Learn DWV (drain-waste-vent) basics and code concepts
Compare service plumbing vs construction plumbing careers
Practice plumbing math (offsets, grades, volumes)

resources.title: BLS OOH — Plumbers, Pipefitters, and Steamfitters

detail.description: HVACR technicians install and service heating, cooling, and refrigeration systems — trade school or apprenticeship, EPA Section 608 certification (federally required to handle refrigerants), then specialization.
detail.why: HVAC combines electrical, mechanical, and diagnostic skill with steady replacement demand and strong self-employment potential.
learn: Plan for EPA 608 certification early (required by federal law)
Learn refrigeration cycle basics and electrical diagnostics
Compare residential service vs commercial install careers
Note NATE-style excellence credentials as later polish

certs.name: EPA Section 608 Certification
certs.note: Federal certification required to service refrigerant-containing equipment; types I–IV by equipment class.

resources.title: BLS OOH — HVACR Mechanics and Installers

detail.description: Welders join metal across construction, manufacturing, shipyards, and pipelines — trade school or employer training plus process-specific certifications (AWS) and heavy specialization (TIG, pipe, structural).
detail.why: Welding skill is portable and certifiable; top specialists (pipe, underwater, aerospace-adjacent) command strong premiums.
learn: Compare the main processes: SMAW, MIG, TIG
Find a welding program with certification testing on site
Understand AWS certification structure basics
Note specialty paths: pipe welding, inspection (CWI) later

resources.title: O*NET — Welders, Cutters, Solderers, and Brazers

detail.description: Automotive service technicians diagnose and repair vehicles — postsecondary programs or dealership apprenticeships, then ASE certification series by system area, with EV/electronics as the growth frontier.
detail.why: Diagnostics-driven work suits problem solvers; EV transition is pulling the trade toward electronics and software-adjacent skills.
learn: Learn the ASE certification series (A1–A9 style areas)
Compare dealership, independent shop, and fleet employers
Build core tool budget awareness (it is real)
Follow EV/hybrid service training requirements early

certs.name: ASE Certification
certs.issuer: National Institute for Automotive Service Excellence
certs.note: Series of system-area exams (brakes, engine, electrical…) with work-experience prerequisites; recertification every five years.

resources.title: O*NET — Automotive Service Technicians and Mechanics

detail.description: Construction laborers support sites across trades — the classic entry point to discover which specialty fits, often with employer-paid training and union apprenticeship options afterward.
detail.why: It pays to learn site culture, tools, and safety while deciding which licensed trade to pursue.
learn: Get OSHA 10 first — most sites require it
Learn common tools and site cleanup standards
Observe which trades you'd want to join from the inside
Ask about apprenticeship sponsorships from employers

resources.title: BLS OOH — Construction Laborers and Helpers

detail.description: Journeyman is the licensed professional tier in the licensed trades: completed apprenticeship hours plus a state exam covering code and practical knowledge. It means unsupervised work.
detail.why: The journeyman card is the trade's degree — it unlocks full pay rates and is the prerequisite for master and contractor tiers.
learn: Confirm your state's OJT-hour and classroom requirements
Get your hours documented and signed from day one
Study your state's code-based exam outline deliberately
Plan the exam application timeline with your program

detail.description: Master status (in electrical and plumbing especially) requires additional years and a harder exam covering design and supervision — it qualifies you to plan systems, pull permits in many jurisdictions, and supervise.
detail.why: Master licenses open estimator, superintendent, inspector, and contractor-owner doors.
learn: Check whether your state/county uses master tiers and their requirements
Log supervisory and design-adjacent experience early
Prepare for code-depth exam questions with a prep course
Ask mentors what master status changed for them

detail.description: A contractor license lets you run your own business: state registration or exam (varies widely), bonding and insurance, and responsibility for permits, employees, and warranties.
detail.why: Ownership is the main wealth path in the trades — and it runs on craft credibility plus business skill.
learn: Research your state's contractor licensing and exam
Learn bonding, liability insurance, and workers' comp basics
Study estimating and job costing before bidding
Talk to an owner about the first two years' reality

detail.description: Beyond licenses, trades stack certifications: EPA 608 for refrigerants, ASE for vehicles, AWS for welding, manufacturer training for equipment, and backflow/medical-gas endorsements in piping.
detail.why: Certifications raise your rate, expand the jobs you can legally do, and often come with employer-paid training.
learn: List the certifications your target trade values most
Ask employers which they pay for
Schedule one certification per quarter while working
Track renewals in a simple calendar

detail.description: Field leadership: foremen run crews and daily schedules; superintendents run entire sites — schedule, subcontractors, safety, and owner relationships.
detail.why: Leadership track tradespeople multiply their value without leaving the field they love.
learn: Volunteer to lead small crews and material coordination
Learn reading construction schedules (lookahead planning)
Practice the daily huddle and end-of-day report
Study how superintendents manage subcontractor coordination

detail.description: Experienced tradespeople branch into code inspection (municipal or third-party), apprenticeship instruction, warranty and field-trainer roles, and technical sales for tools and materials.
detail.why: These roles trade some field pay for physical longevity and steady schedules — a real second act built on your expertise.
learn: Check your municipality's inspector requirements (often master-level)
Explore teaching at trade schools (experience-based hiring)
Consider manufacturer field-trainer and tech-rep roles
Note inspector certification options in your trade

detail.description: Service trades live or die on trust: explaining problems in plain language, giving options with prices, showing up when promised, and leaving spaces clean.
detail.why: Communication is the highest-leverage skill for independent tradespeople — it is the difference between a job and a customer for life.
learn: Practice explaining one repair two ways: technical and plain
Build an options presentation: fix now / fix later / replace
Follow the walk-through-then-clean standard every job
Ask every customer for a review at completion

detail.description: Owning a trade business means estimating, scheduling, cash flow, hiring helpers, and marketing — roughly half the job once you're the owner.
detail.why: Owners capture the margin labor doesn't; the business side is learnable and compounds for decades.
learn: Learn job costing: labor, materials, overhead, margin
Set up simple quoting and invoicing workflows
Understand payroll and workers' comp obligations
Build a simple marketing engine: reviews + referrals + local presence

detail.description: The standard ladder: helper/apprentice → journeyman → master/foreman → superintendent, contractor-owner, inspector, or instructor — with earnings rising at each licensed tier.
detail.why: Unlike many careers, trades ladders are visible and license-gated: you can see exactly what the next rung requires.
learn: Map your state's tiers for your trade
Set a target tier and its hour/exam requirements
Find two mentors a rung ahead of you
Revisit the plan yearly as your body and interests change

resources.title: BLS OOH — Installation, Maintenance, and Repair

detail.description: Trades are physical careers: knees, backs, and hearing need deliberate care — technique, PPE, strength work, and honest decisions about moving toward inspection, supervision, or ownership with age.
detail.why: The tradespeople who thrive for 30+ years planned for longevity from year one, not after the first injury.
learn: Learn proper lifting and positioning technique early
Invest in knee/back protection and hearing protection habitually
Keep a simple strength and mobility routine
Plan your physical-to-mentally-weighted career shift timeline

detail.description: Union apprenticeships offer structured training, scale wages, and benefits; open shop offers faster responsibility and ownership paths. Both build excellent tradespeople — the choice is cultural and financial.
detail.why: Which system you enter shapes your training quality, network, and business options — worth deciding deliberately.
learn: Compare local union apprenticeship wages/benefits vs open shop
Interview one person from each system
Note how licensing differs (it doesn't — but access does)
Choose based on your learning style and local market

detail.description: Programs actively recruit beyond the stereotype: pre-apprenticeship programs, women-in-trades organizations, veterans' programs (Helmets to Hardhats), and second-career entrants are all common paths.
detail.why: Trades shortages mean programs want motivated entrants of every background — support networks exist for yours.
learn: Look for pre-apprenticeship programs in your area
Check veterans' pathway programs if applicable
Connect with trades-community organizations for your background
Use career-change programs that fund tools and training
